migration.migration_reason: A preserved paid Semantic Compression metric shard with the same scientific experiment identity as the recertified owner was rebound to the current canonical catalog. Explicit legacy fragments, when present, matched exactly; the current metric validator re-checks the result.

metric.hidden_semantic_cost.basis: all-fragments (Python-only shard; common-basis reconciliation across languages is performed by the runner when all language shards are merged)

counting_methodology.aggregation: raw_total = sum(per-probe counts) over the 41 measured (non-NONE) probes for Python. avg_hidden_per_probe = raw_total / n_measured. Normalized score (higher=better, 0-100) = 100 * (1 - avg_hidden_per_probe / 9), i.e. the theoretical worst case (all 9 categories triggered on every probe) maps to 0 and zero hidden behavior on every probe maps to 100.
counting_methodology.caveat: This figure is produced by a single Python-only worker shard per the assigned requirement id and language. It has not been cross-validated against the other nine language shards and does not itself constitute the common-basis Hidden Semantic Cost comparison table entry; the runner must intersect this with the other languages' NONE/PARTIAL/FULL support levels before computing the common-basis figure required by interaction_with_quality_metrics.
counting_methodology.rule: For each probe with a Python fragment authored under R1-R10 (idiomatic, minimal, fixed identifiers), each of the 9 checklist categories is scored 1 if the fragment's SURFACE FORM permits that behavior to occur WITHOUT a locally-evident syntactic signal (per spec D: 'Do not count a behavior as hidden if the fixed local syntax makes that behavior unambiguous under the language specification'), else 0. A single underlying language rule is counted once per probe even if it could be described under more than one category (no double counting within one probe). Per-probe raw score is an integer 0-9 (count of triggered categories). This is a single-annotator pass; it is reproducible from the fragment text and the categories listed, and is published per-probe below for audit.

excluded_probes.F04.P1: NONE - Python has no documented mechanism for a second name to hold writable access to an existing scalar local; ints are immutable and there is no reference/pointer/inout form for a bare scalar. Not in the R9 named-substitution list, so no fragment is written (rubric N-1).
excluded_probes.F05.P2: NONE - Python provides no documented mechanism for a callee to write a caller's scalar local variable (no pass-by-reference for scalars); wrapping in a mutable container is explicitly disallowed as a FULL/PARTIAL substitute by the probe's own text. No fragment written (rubric N-1).
excluded_probes.F20.P2: NONE - the frozen Python recipe (`python3 FILE.py`) produces no compiled artifact, so no unmangled C-ABI symbol can be verified with `nm`. Recorded as NONE with reason 'no compiled artifact under the frozen recipe' per na_policy rule NA-6 / support_rubric N-1, not as N/A.

F01.P1.note: `n = 7; return n` has no immutable-binding form in Python; the name is always rebindable with no syntactic marker distinguishing intended non-reassignment. Small-int allocation/caching is implicit.

F01.P2.note: `LIMIT = 100` is a naming convention only; Python enforces no true constant, so LIMIT remains reassignable from any code in the unit with no compiler diagnostic.

F02.P1.note: Python performs no static definite-assignment analysis; if a future edit misses a branch, reading `v` raises UnboundLocalError at runtime with no signal at the declaration site (there is no declaration site).

F02.P2.note: Substituted default-initialized `bytearray(16)` (Python has no true uninitialized-buffer primitive, R9 substitution, PARTIAL). Element assignment silently wraps/truncates any out-of-range int mod 256 with no local signal.

F03.P1.note: `x += 1` on an int rebinds `x` to a newly allocated int object (ints are immutable); the compound-assignment syntax visually suggests in-place mutation but performs allocation+rebind.

F03.P2.note: `xs[1] = 42` can raise IndexError if `xs` is shorter than expected; the syntax gives no local signal that this is a fallible operation.

F04.P2.note: Python has no read-only view type for a plain list; `window = xs` aliases the full list and IS writable through `window`, contradicting the probe's read-only intent (PARTIAL under P-a). This is a hidden mutation risk not signaled at the binding site.

F04.P3.note: `same = first is second` is Python's explicit, unambiguous identity operator; no hidden category applies.

F05.P1.note: Bare call `f(x)` passes the list object by reference with no sigil; the callee may read, mutate elements, resize, or retain the alias, none of which is visible at the call site. `f` itself is resolved dynamically (any name rebinding/monkeypatch changes behavior) and is not locally evident.

F05.P3.note: Python closures are late-binding: `neg` captures the cell holding `k`, not `k`'s value at definition time; if `k` were later reassigned before the map runs, `neg`'s behavior would silently change, with no local signal.

F06.P1.note: `return xs[1]` returns the element object itself (no copy); if the element is itself mutable, `y` and the original element remain aliased with no local signal distinguishing this from a value copy.

F06.P2.note: Returning `(a // b, a % b)` implicitly allocates a tuple object with no syntax marking allocation; `a // b` / `a % b` can raise ZeroDivisionError, which Python's untyped signature never signals.

F07.P1.note: `r = a * b + c` on Python's arbitrary-precision ints has standard, unambiguous, well-known precedence and no overflow behavior to hide.

F07.P2.note: `d = a / b` implicitly promotes both operands to float with no explicit conversion syntax; all three operators can raise ZeroDivisionError with no signature-level signal; Python's `%` takes the sign of the divisor (floor-modulo), a behavior not evident from the operator alone and different from truncating-remainder languages.

F08.P1.note: Python ints have no fixed width, so modeling a signed-32-bit overflow requires a substitution via `ctypes.c_int32(...).value`, which silently truncates/wraps mod 2**32; the wrap behavior is a property of the ctypes wrapper type, not evident from the arithmetic expression itself.

F08.P2.note: The explicit `0 if b == 0 else a // b` guard (rung ii) makes the zero-divisor case fully explicit and non-hidden, but `//`'s floor-toward-negative-infinity rounding for negative operands remains a context-dependent numeric behavior not evident from the operator alone.

F09.P1.note: `s1 == s2` dispatches to `__eq__`, which is dynamically resolved and may be overridden by a subclass; the operator site gives no local signal of which `__eq__` implementation runs.

F09.P2.note: `xs.sort(reverse=True)` (R10 fewest-tokens form) mutates `xs` in place; this is easily confused with `sorted(xs, reverse=True)` which does not, and the in-place mutation of pre-existing state is not obvious purely from the method name at the call site without prior knowledge of the distinction.

F10.P1.note: Narrowing to 32 bits requires the substitution `ctypes.c_int32(big).value`, which performs a silent masking/representation change with no visible truncation syntax at the assignment.

F10.P2.note: `sum = i + d` implicitly widens the int operand to float; no explicit conversion call appears in the expression.

F11.P1.note: `e = xs[i]` can raise IndexError for out-of-range `i`; ordinary indexing syntax carries no type-level or local signal that the operation is fallible.

F11.P2.note: `part = xs[1:4]` ALWAYS COPIES the sliced elements into a new list object in Python (unlike e.g. NumPy array views); this copy is not evident from the slicing syntax, which looks identical to a view operation in other languages/libraries.

F12.P1.note: Python has no runtime-enforced Optional type; any variable, regardless of type hints, may hold None at any point, and this is never enforced or signaled beyond an unchecked, erasable type annotation.

F12.P2.note: Same underlying gap as F12.P1: the substituted explicit-conditional form (Python has no optional-chaining operator, R9 substitution, PARTIAL) still relies on an unenforced None-vs-value distinction.

F13.P1.note: `parse_twice`'s signature carries no indication that `int(s)` can raise ValueError and propagate to the caller; Python has no checked-exception declaration mechanism.

F13.P2.note: `try: n = int(s) except ValueError: n = 0` makes the protected operation and the failure path fully explicit and local; no hidden category applies.

F14.P1.note: Declaring `Circle`/`Rect` dataclasses and constructing `Circle(2.0)` involves no checklist-covered hidden behavior at this specific site (the lack of closedness enforcement is a capability-coverage fact, not one of the 9 hidden-behavior checklist categories).

F14.P2.note: Python's `match`/`case` performs runtime structural/type-based dispatch with no compile-time exhaustiveness check; dispatch resolution is not locally evident, and if no case matches, the statement silently falls through with NO error at all (a silent-failure mode not signaled anywhere in the construct).

F14.P3.note: Dispatch to `Tri.area()` from a separate unit is pure duck-typing dynamic dispatch; there is no interface declaration at the call site confirming which implementation runs.

F15.P1.note: `head(xs)` works unconstrained via duck typing by design (the probe itself is the unconstrained case); no additional hidden category is triggered beyond what F15.P1 intentionally tests.

F15.P2.note: Python cannot enforce a declaration-site comparability constraint (R9 substitution, PARTIAL); a call with non-comparable types is only diagnosed as a TypeError at the call site, never at `max_of`'s declaration.

F15.P3.note: `items[0].tag()` dispatches on the runtime type of the concrete object with no interface check; nothing at the call site names which concrete implementation executes.

F16.P1.note: `xs = [1, 2, 3]; total = sum(xs)` uses well-documented, unambiguous standard-library behavior; no hidden category applies.

F16.P2.note: Dict iteration order is a documented guarantee (insertion order) since Python 3.7, and `mp.get('b', 0)` makes the missing-key fallback fully explicit; no hidden category applies.

F17.P1.note: `open(...)` can raise OSError/FileNotFoundError; the `with` statement guarantees deterministic close on every exit path (this itself is NOT hidden), but the possible-failure nature of the open call is not signaled by the construct's type.

F17.P2.note: `__del__` is documented as NOT a deterministic destructor guarantee at the language-specification level (CPython's refcounting usually triggers it promptly, but this is an implementation detail, not a language guarantee, and fails under reference cycles or alternate implementations); a reader relying on the surface form alone would wrongly assume determinism.

F18.P1.note: `print('x')` is a builtin needing no import and has fully documented, unambiguous behavior.

F18.P2.note: No checklist category directly covers unenforced-privacy-convention (leading underscore); this gap is captured elsewhere (capability coverage / R9 substitution), not by the 9-item hidden-behavior checklist.

F19.P1.note: Thread or task objects created via `concurrent.futures`/`threading` involve implicit allocation and implicit cleanup of OS-level thread resources not marked by the launch syntax.

F19.P2.note: `with lock: counter += 1` makes the synchronization discipline fully explicit and local; no hidden category applies.

F20.P1.note: `ctypes.CDLL(None).abs(-3)` without explicit `argtypes`/`restype` declarations silently assumes C `int`-sized arguments and return value; a well-documented ctypes footgun where mismatched underlying signatures silently corrupt values with no local signal.
